patient_information: A 45-year-old male security guard from Malawi with no history of past tuberculosis. He is a non-smoker but drinks about one litre of Chibuku, a locally brewed beer, per day. He has never been tested for HIV before this illness. He is married with three children who are all well.
chief_complaint: Back pain and progressive difficulty in walking for one year.
history_of_present_illness: The patient's troubles began one year prior to admission with back pain. Over the following weeks, he developed difficulty walking and a 'pins and needles' sensation in his legs. His condition progressively deteriorated over the next six months, and he ultimately became bedridden. The patient denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, chronic cough, haematuria, or diarrhoea. He is continent for stool and urine. There is no history of trauma.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient resides in an urban area in Malawi. He previously worked as a security guard but has been unemployed for the last 6 months due to his illness. During his illness, he consulted a local traditional healer who applied tattoos to his chest and back. He drinks locally brewed beer daily.
vitals: On admission to the tertiary hospital, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Three months after his symptoms began, during a visit to a local health centre, his temperature was slightly elevated at 37.5°C (99.5°F).
physical_exam: The patient looks well. There is tenderness over the lower thoracic spine. Neurological examination reveals severe spasticity of both legs with power of 1/5 (visible muscle flicker). Deep tendon reflexes of the lower limbs are exaggerated and plantar reflexes are upgoing. A sensory level for pain and temperature sensation is present between T9 and T11, with diminished joint sense in his big toes bilaterally. The examination of his cranial nerves and upper limbs is normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count results were normal. The patient was found to be HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 331 cells/μL. His urine dipstick was normal, and no ova of Schistosoma spp. were detected in his urine and stool. A spinal radiograph showed a collapse of the T11 vertebral body as well as soft tissue swelling around the spine. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound examination were normal.
differential_diagnosis: The clinical presentation localized the lesion to the spinal cord. The differential diagnosis for non-traumatic compressive spinal cord disease in this setting included spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease), spinal metastases, and degenerative spinal disease. Non-compressive causes considered were schistosomiasis, autoimmune transverse myelitis, and HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy.
management_and_clinical_course: A presumed diagnosis of spinal TB was made, and the patient was started on standard first-line antituberculous treatment along with Vitamin B6. He was also initiated on antiretroviral therapy for HIV. Physiotherapy and intensive guardian counselling were provided. A spinal surgeon did not recommend surgical intervention at that time. At a 4-week follow-up, his neurological deficits were unchanged. At 3 months, he reported some subjective improvement in his gait, but his clinical deficits remained unchanged. He was taking his antituberculous and antiretroviral medication regularly.
final_diagnosis: The patient was diagnosed with presumed spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease). This diagnosis was based on the clinical syndrome of chronic, progressive spastic paraparesis with a thoracic sensory level, supported by spinal radiograph findings showing a collapse of the T11 vertebral body and surrounding soft tissue swelling. The diagnosis was made in the context of his newly diagnosed HIV-positive status in a TB-endemic region. Schistosomiasis was considered less likely after urine and stool tests were negative for ova.
